Robert Echlin
rob'ert ek'lin
n. (Robert Echlin, 1576–1635, bishop of Down and Connor)
Germanic Hrodberht, bright in fame, through Robert; Scottish Echlin, from a Fife family name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Robert Echlin was a Scot, bishop of Down and Connor from 1613, and for nearly twenty years he did something quietly remarkable: he ordained and tolerated in his diocese the Scots Presbyterian ministers of the Ulster plantation, men who would not use the whole English liturgy, because they were preaching and his people needed preaching. Under those men the revival at Six Mile Water broke out in 1625. Then the pressure came from Dublin and from Laud, and in 1631 Echlin silenced four of them, including Robert Blair and John Livingstone. He died four years later. The dictionary gives the record whole, and the whole of it is a case study in the cost of a quiet accommodation made without a principle to defend it (Pro 29:25).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines connivance as voluntary blindness to an act, and suspension as a temporary removal from office.

expand to see more

CONNI'VANCE, n. Voluntary blindness to an act; intentional forbearance to see a fault or other act, generally implying consent.

SUSPEN'SION, n. A temporary removal of a person from the exercise of an office; the act of debarring from a privilege.

TOLERA'TION, n. The allowance of that which is not wholly approved; the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.

REVI'VAL, n. Renewed and more active attention to religion; the awakening of men to a sense of their condition.

Modern Corruption

Twenty years of quiet toleration, a revival under it, and four ministers silenced at the end.

expand to see more

The dictionary names the weakness without discounting the good done. For twenty years Echlin let the Presbyterian preachers work, and the Six Mile Water awakening and the churches that grew out of it are the fruit of that forbearance. But it was forbearance, not conviction. He had never defended it on principle, so when the pressure came he had nothing to stand on and he silenced the very men whose ministry had filled his churches.

The principle to recover is that a position held only by convenience will not hold under pressure, and the fear of man is the ordinary mechanism. “The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe” (Pro 29:25). The apostles' answer to the same pressure was a settled one: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). And the harvest those men were reaping was real: “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing” (Psa 126:6).
